newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Giordano languishes in China woes.
newsitem.headline: Giordano languishes in China woes.

text.p: Buyers of Giordano shares have nurtured hopes that the Hong Kong retailer would make some headway with its plans to expand into China, but the latest news from the company has only heightened uncertainty, analysts said on Monday.

Giordano International Ltd shares plunged nearly 25 percent on Monday after the company said negotations to set up new outlets in Beijing and Shanghai had not been concluded and the company was continuing to address regulatory procedural demands concerning its China operations.
The stock fell HK$1.25 to close at HK$3.80, after slipping to their lowest level since Spring 1994 at HK$3.525.
"Some of these guys have paid high prices for this stock in the past and are increasingly getting disillusioned with the story," said Alan Hutcheson, director of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Giordano's Chinese expansion first hit a snag in August 1994 when its flagship China store in Beijing was closed by officials due to licensing problems. Most analysts believed, however, it had something to do with founder Jimmy Lai's vitriolic comments about Chinese premier Li Peng in his Next Magazine.
Lai subsequently stepped down from the board as chairman and placed out his entire shareholding in the company in early 1996.
But unfavourable rumours on Giordano's China expansion did not go away.
The company then said last week it had appointed N.M. Rothschild & Sons (Hong Kong) Ltd to advise it on its business in China and related issues.

Giordano then said on Monday it was in active negotiations with certain Chinese enterprises for joint venture arrangements for the group's China operations and was seeking strategic investors to beef up its bussiness in China and other markets.
Analysts also said the company announcement gave very little information. "There is little if any value in these releases. They haven't told the market anything," one said.
Monday's sell off was mainly due to uncertainties, analysts said.
"There is a lot of speculation that they are not able to operate in the China market," the analyst said.

Howard Gorges, director at South China Brokerage, said the announcements did not come as a big surprise. "I think poeple got a bit carried away a few months ago. Now you have got to discount quite a lot of that growth potential," he said.

Another analyst said sentiment has been damaged by the lack of transparency of the company's management. "It's a wild card. You don't know what's going on. They have not been very open about how things have been probably going through," he said.
"Even if they can pull something together, it's a major problem looking forward in the management credibility."
But one analyst with a European house said Monday's fall was overdone since the China problem was not new.

"Definitely they are having problems now. Look at 1996, they had problems in 1996 and they managed to open 31 more outlets," she said, adding that the management was addressing the problems and was confident they could be resolved.
"The company is trying to do something about it but it is not happening quickly and that is a big concern particulary for foreign investors," added Hutcheson.
